paras: The threatened lynching of R. H. Kruger was a reported threat of mob violence against a man arrested in Chicago on October 18, 1888, on a charge of assaulting a girl in Grand Rapids, Michigan. A Chicago wire dispatch quoted a Grand Rapids deputy sheriff as saying Kruger would be lynched if brought back, but no crowd or attack was reported, and a Michigan paper recorded his court appearance the next day without mentioning any threat. Accounts differed over the age and identity of the complainant, and Kruger was later released.

Kruger, whose name the papers printed as R. H. Kreuger, R. H. Kruger, A. H. Kruger and R. K. Kruger, was described in one dispatch as "a respectable-looking man of 30 years" from Grand Rapids. According to the Chicago dispatches, he was accused of "outraging" twelve-year-old Louisa McKay. The Rock Island Argus version added that he had taken her riding in a buggy several days earlier, assaulted her in a secluded place in the suburbs, and that the child was "not expected to recover."

Kruger was arrested in Chicago on the morning of October 18 on a telegram from Grand Rapids, as he was about to take a train for Portland, Oregon. At the central police station, the deputy sent to bring him back, named Shaley in the wire story, was quoted as saying, "If I take the villain back to Grand Rapids he will be lynched before I can get him safely locked up." He added that the whole town was "up in arms" and that 10,000 people would be at the depot if they knew he had the prisoner.

These statements are the only source for the threat, and no report describes a crowd gathering in Grand Rapids. On October 19, according to the Telegram-Herald, Kruger appeared before Justice Westfall, demanded an examination, and had his case adjourned until the following Wednesday.

By the end of October Kruger had been released, though the coverage does not say how the charge was disposed of, and no report of a trial was found. After his release, a letter signed H. R. Kruger of Chicago appeared in the Democrat attacking Sheriff Bishop, apparently over his treatment and his money and effects. Replies printed in the Telegram-Herald on November 1, during a campaign in which L. T. Kinney opposed Bishop, defended the sheriff. One correspondent, signing "Justice," wrote that "no man received better treatment under a similar charge than said Kruger," and another, John F. Matthews, said Kruger had claimed Kinney's friends offered him $25 to write the letter.

The lynching threat circulated as a Chicago wire story dated October 18, printed on October 19 by the St. Paul Daily Globe under "He Will Be Lynched" and the subhead "Wolverines Thirst for the Blood of a Ravisher," and by the Memphis Appeal as "They Have the Rope Ready." The Wheeling Register ran it on October 20 as "Thirsting for a Rapist's Blood" under an October 17 dateline, and Baltimore's Der Deutsche Correspondent summarized it in German, saying the city's people threatened to lynch him on his return. The wire version called Kruger "the villain" and a "ravisher" and repeated the telegram's statement that he had been "guilty" of the outrage.

By contrast, the Rock Island Argus headed its separate dispatch "Arrested on a Terrible Charge" and said nothing of lynching. The Telegram-Herald's brief report of the court appearance was matter-of-fact and also did not mention a threat.

The Chicago dispatches named the complainant as twelve-year-old Louisa McKay, while the Telegram-Herald reported that the girl was 22 years old, named Wenzler, and the daughter of McKay's wife by a former husband. The local paper added that McKay said he had forbidden her to go with Kruger. The deputy's name also differed, appearing as Shaley in the wire story and Scally in the Telegram-Herald.
